title: Westsource Group Holdings Inc. (Jan 2017 TCC) Decision
subject: TCC appeal on whether omitting Form T661 lines 240, 242, and 244 barred an SR&ED claim under s. 37(11).
summary: Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 9, affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in 2018 FCA 57, confirms that Canadian corporations claiming SR&ED tax credits under the Income Tax Act must file a complete Form T661, including technical project narratives, within twelve months of their filing-due date; omissions permanently disqualify the claim.
metaDescription: Analyze the January 2017 Tax Court of Canada decision for Westsource Group Holdings Inc. on Canadian SR&ED tax credit claims.

body.text: Executive Summary & Case Background

The jurisprudence governing Canada’s Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program establishes a rigid demarcation between substantive technical eligibility and procedural statutory compliance. In Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 9 (Docket: 2015-3982(IT)G), handed down on January 24, 2017, by the Honourable Justice Valerie A. Miller of the Tax Court of Canada—and subsequently affirmed unanimously from the bench by the Federal Court of Appeal in Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. Canada, 2018 FCA 57—the Canadian judiciary reinforced that the statutory filing requirements under subsections 37(11) and 37(12) of the federal Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "Act") operate as an absolute, non-discretionary bar to entitlement. The decision confirms that a taxpayer’s failure to populate the technical project narrative fields on Form T661 prior to the twelve-month statutory filing deadline is permanently fatal to an SR&ED claim, even where the taxpayer contends that the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) could have found the missing project information in the Form T661 filed by a related corporation that collaborated on the same project, and that the related corporation’s claims for that project had been accepted by the Minister.
The Taxpayer's Claim and Factual Matrix

Westsource Group Holdings Inc. (the "Appellant" or "Westsource") is a privately held corporation based in Saskatchewan whose principal business activity consists of providing management services to its subsidiary companies. When Westsource initially filed its T2 Corporation Income Tax Return for its 2011 taxation year, it did not report any SR&ED expenditures or claim any associated Investment Tax Credits (ITCs). Prior to the expiration of its statutory SR&ED reporting deadline, Westsource filed an amended return for its 2011 taxation year. In that amended filing, the Appellant submitted Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) reporting SR&ED expenditures across two distinct projects and claiming refundable ITCs of $29,504 in respect of Project 1 and $26,894 in respect of Project 2.

In preparing Part 2 of Form T661 (designated as Schedule 60 to the T2 return), the Appellant fully completed the technical project narrative fields in Boxes 240, 242, and 244 for Project 2. Conversely, for Project 1, while the Appellant reported the financial expenditure figures on the form, it left Boxes 240, 242, and 244 of Schedule 60 entirely blank. According to counsel for the Appellant at the hearing, the underlying activities of Project 1 (described as "WSG P01 Multiple Aspect Wind Turbine Development") involved a collaboration between the Appellant and WestSource Solutions Inc., a corporation related to the Appellant. Crucially, counsel argued that the Minister could have found the missing prescribed information for the Appellant by looking at the Form T661 filed on behalf of WestSource Solutions Inc., and, before the Federal Court of Appeal, Westsource submitted that the related corporation’s claims for the project had been accepted by the Minister; however, the Minister did not complete a detailed technical review or financial review of the Appellant’s Project 1.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

Upon reviewing Westsource’s amended 2011 tax return, the Minister of National Revenue (the "Minister") reassessed the Appellant under the Act. Project 2 was accepted as filed without a review, and the Minister granted the Appellant the refundable ITC of $26,894 claimed for that project, Schedule 60 having been completed for Project 2. However, the Minister disallowed the $29,504 refundable ITC claimed for Project 1 in its entirety.

The Minister’s reassessment was not predicated on a substantive technical determination that Project 1 failed to meet the scientific criteria of SR&ED; rather, the Minister denied the claim strictly on procedural grounds. Specifically, the Crown asserted that by omitting the technical narratives required in Boxes 240, 242, and 244 of Schedule 60 of Form T661, Westsource failed to comply with the mandatory statutory requirement under subsections 37(11) and 37(12) (and paragraph 127(9)(m) in respect of ITCs) to file a "prescribed form containing prescribed information in respect of the expenditure" within twelve months after its corporate filing-due date for the 2011 taxation year.
Governing Statutory Framework in Canada

The adjudication of Westsource’s appeal turned on the integrated operation of several statutory provisions within the Income Tax Act. At the substantive foundation of the regime, subsection 248(1) of the Act defines "scientific research and experimental development" as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that is basic research or applied research (work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge) or experimental development (work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement), and includes the commensurate support work described in paragraph (d) that is directly in support of work described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c). As summarized by Justice Miller in Westsource (citing 6379249 Canada Inc. v R, 2015 TCC 77 at paragraph 59), a taxpayer must establish three criteria before its project will be accepted as SR&ED: scientific or technological uncertainty, a systematic investigation carried out in a field of technology by means of experiment or analysis, and work undertaken for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement. Where those substantive criteria are met, subsection 37(1) permits a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada to deduct qualifying SR&ED expenditures of a current nature (and, for taxation years prior to 2014, capital nature) from business income while placing those expenditures into a permanent tax pool, whereas subsections 127(5) and 127(9) govern the calculation and deduction of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits, and section 127.1 governs the refundable portion of those credits for qualifying corporations, including Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) meeting statutory thresholds.

Entitlement to both the subsection 37(1) deduction and the subsection 127(5) ITC is conditioned upon strict statutory filing rules. Subsection 37(11) mandates that a taxpayer must file with the Minister a prescribed form containing prescribed information in respect of an SR&ED expenditure on or before the day that is twelve months after the taxpayer's filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred. Because a corporation’s filing-due date under paragraph 150(1)(a) is six months after the end of its taxation year, subsection 37(11) creates an absolute eighteen-month window following fiscal year-end to file a complete Form T661. Paragraph 127(9)(m) imposes an identical twelve-month post-filing-due-date limitation period for filing the prescribed form (Schedule T2SCH31 and Form T661) in order for an expenditure to qualify for ITCs.

The statutory consequence of failing to satisfy subsection 37(11) is governed by an explicit deeming rule. During the 2011 taxation year at issue in Westsource, subsection 37(11) itself provided that no amount in respect of the expenditure could be deducted under subsection 37(1) unless the taxpayer filed a prescribed form containing prescribed information within the deadline, and subsection 37(12) provided that if a taxpayer had not filed a prescribed form in respect of an expenditure in accordance with subsection 37(11), the expenditure was deemed, for the purposes of the Act, not to be an expenditure on or in respect of SR&ED. Subsequent legislative amendments to the Act—introduced alongside the claim preparer penalty regime in subsection 162(5.1), with "claim preparer information" defined in subsection 162(5.3)—restructured these provisions into paragraph 37(11)(a) (requiring prescribed information in respect of the expenditure), paragraph 37(11)(b) (requiring claim preparer information), and subsection 37(11.1) (housing the strict deduction-denial rule previously embedded directly in subsection 37(11)), while retaining the deeming rule in subsection 37(12) and the identical substantive penalty of total expenditure disqualification.

Finally, the statutory mechanism linking Form T661 to subsection 37(11) rests, as Justice Miller held, on the definition of "prescribed" in subsection 248(1) of the Act, with subsection 244(16) providing supplementary statutory context. Subsection 248(1) bifurcates the definition of the term "prescribed": in the case of a form, the information to be given on a form, or the manner of filing a form, "prescribed" means authorized by the Minister; in any other case, it means prescribed by regulation or determined in accordance with rules prescribed by regulation. Subsection 244(16), which was not relied upon in the Tax Court’s reasons, supplements this delegation by deeming every form purporting to be a form prescribed or authorized by the Minister to be a form authorized under the Act by the Minister unless called in question by the Minister or by a person acting for the Minister or Her Majesty.
The Court's Final Holding

Justice Valerie A. Miller dismissed Westsource’s appeal with costs to the Respondent. The Tax Court held that subsection 37(11) is clear and that, under the definition of "prescribed" in subsection 248(1), the information to be given on a prescribed form is "prescribed information". Because Form T661 is a form authorized by the Minister, the information requested on that form constitutes "prescribed information" by operation of law under subsection 248(1), without any requirement for a separate regulation under the Income Tax Regulations. Furthermore, Justice Miller noted that the explicit instructions printed on Form T661 notify taxpayers that all information requested in the form is prescribed information.

The Court concluded that Boxes 240, 242, and 244 of Schedule 60 (which correspond to Lines 242, 244, and 246 in subsequent revisions of Form T661) go directly to the substantive core of whether the claimed activities satisfy the statutory definition of SR&ED under subsection 248(1). By leaving those boxes blank for Project 1, Westsource failed to file a prescribed form containing the prescribed information within the twelve-month statutory deadline. Finally, Justice Miller ruled that the Minister was not required to look into another taxpayer’s file—namely, the Form T661 filed on behalf of WestSource Solutions Inc., with which counsel stated the Appellant had collaborated on Project 1—to ascertain the Appellant’s prescribed information, citing Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd v The Queen, 2016 FCA 301, and further noted that subsection 220(2.2) has removed the Minister’s authority to waive the requirement to provide the prescribed information mandated by subsection 37(11). Upon appeal, the Federal Court of Appeal (per Justice Judith Woods, with Justices Rennie and Laskin concurring) reviewed the Tax Court’s statutory interpretation on a standard of correctness, found no reviewable error, emphasized that tax relief cannot be granted on grounds of fairness alone in the face of clear statutory language, and dismissed the appeal from the bench with costs.
Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

The disqualification of Project 1 in Westsource Group Holdings Inc. was not the result of an adverse scientific peer review during a CRA technical audit, but rather the consequence of compounding legal, technical, corporate-structural, and compliance failures at the filing stage. An exhaustive analysis of the ruling exposes four primary deficiencies that proved fatal to the taxpayer's claim.
Omission of Statutory SR&ED Narrative Elements (Boxes 240, 242, and 244)

The primary evidentiary and technical failure committed by Westsource was the complete omission of project-level technical narratives in Boxes 240, 242, and 244 of Schedule 60 (Part 2 of Form T661) for Project 1. In the version of Form T661 applicable to the 2011 taxation year, Part 2 required the claimant to answer three foundational questions for every claimed project—topics which on later versions of Form T661 are addressed in Lines 242 (uncertainties), 244 (work performed), and 246 (advancements) following the reorganization of the project description sections. Specifically, Box 240 required the taxpayer to state the scientific or technological advancement it attempted to achieve; Box 242 required the taxpayer to describe the scientific or technological obstacles or uncertainties it had to overcome to achieve those advancements; and Box 244 required the taxpayer to detail the exact work performed (the systematic investigation or search) in the taxation year to overcome the technological obstacles or uncertainties identified in Box 242.

As Crown counsel argued before the Tax Court, and as Justice Miller explicitly endorsed, the information required in Boxes 240, 242, and 244 "goes to the heart of whether the claim made is SR&ED". These three boxes are not administrative metadata; as Justice Miller held, they specifically address the three criteria that a taxpayer must establish before its project will be accepted as SR&ED—scientific or technological uncertainty, a systematic investigation by means of experiment or analysis, and work undertaken for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement—as set out in 6379249 Canada Inc. v R, 2015 TCC 77, and thereby give operational effect to the statutory definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the Act. Without Box 242, there is no assertion of technological uncertainty confirming that standard engineering or routine practice could not resolve the problem. Without Box 244, there is no record of a systematic investigation or search carried out by means of experiment or analysis during the specific taxation year. Without Box 240, there is no identification of the new scientific knowledge or technological advancement sought. By submitting financial expenditure numbers on Form T661 while leaving Schedule 60 blank for Project 1, Westsource filed a bare accounting claim devoid of any prima facie technical foundation.
Misconstruction of "Prescribed Information" Under the Income Tax Act

To salvage its defective filing at the Tax Court and the Federal Court of Appeal, counsel for Westsource advanced a technical statutory interpretation argument regarding the meaning of "prescribed information" in subsection 37(11). The Appellant contended that subsections 37(11) and 248(1) draw a distinction between a "prescribed form" and "prescribed information". Relying on the second branch of the definition of "prescribed" in subsection 248(1)—which states that "in any other case, prescribed by regulation or determined in accordance with rules prescribed by regulation"—Westsource argued that because no regulations or rules prescribed by regulation had been made with respect to the phrase "prescribed information" for the purposes of subsections 37(11) and 127(9), there was no "prescribed information" for those purposes, and the narrative boxes in Schedule 60 could not legally be treated as mandatory prescribed information. Before the Tax Court, the Appellant further argued that the purpose of the SR&ED incentives is to allow Canadian businesses to make advancements in science and technology, so that "prescribed information" should be interpreted liberally; before the Federal Court of Appeal, it submitted that the scope of prescribed information was not clear in either the legislation or administrative policy statements, and that budgetary material showed the purpose of the filing requirement was simply to deny retroactive claims for these tax incentives.

Both the Tax Court and the Federal Court of Appeal dismantled this legal argument. Justice Miller pointed directly to the first branch of the definition of "prescribed" in subsection 248(1) of the Act, which explicitly governs "in the case of a form, the information to be given on a form or the manner of filing a form" and defines it as "authorized by the Minister". Justice Miller further held that the Appellant’s interpretation would effectively ignore the term "prescribed information" altogether, contrary to the rule against tautology, under which all words in a statute must be given meaning (Canada (Canadian Human Rights Commission) v Canada (Attorney General), 2011 SCC 53 at paragraph 38). Any field included on a form authorized by the Minister is, ipso facto, "prescribed information". Furthermore, Justice Miller noted at paragraph 27 of her reasons that the instructions on Form T661 clearly state that the information requested in the form and documents supporting the expenditures are prescribed information. The Federal Court of Appeal concurred, holding that the legislation is clear that prescribed information includes information necessary to determine whether the activity qualifies as SR&ED, that this interpretation is consistent with the administrative policy statements to which it was referred, and that a general statement of legislative intent in budget material cannot take precedence over clear, unambiguous statutory language.
Improper Reliance on Intra-Group Collaboration and Constructive Notice

A critical structural failure in Westsource arose from the relationship between the Appellant (a management company providing management services to its subsidiaries) and WestSource Solutions Inc., a related corporation with which, according to the Appellant’s counsel, it collaborated on Project 1. Westsource argued that the Minister could have found the missing prescribed information for Boxes 240, 242, and 244 if he had looked at the Form T661 filed on behalf of WestSource Solutions Inc., and, before the Federal Court of Appeal, submitted that the missing information was not important to its claim because the Minister was already in possession of the relevant information, the related corporation’s claims for the same project having been accepted by the Minister. In essence, the Appellant asserted a doctrine of constructive compliance or administrative notice: because the Minister already possessed the relevant technical information in another taxpayer's file, requiring Westsource to duplicate those narratives on its own Form T661 was redundant.

This argument failed because, as Justice Miller held, subsection 37(11) is clear: the taxpayer seeking to claim an SR&ED expenditure must itself file the prescribed information with the Minister. Unlike jurisdictions that permit consolidated corporate group tax returns, the Canadian Income Tax Act treats every corporation—including a parent management company and its wholly owned operating subsidiary—as a separate and distinct taxpayer. Subsection 37(11) states that "the taxpayer" must file a prescribed form containing prescribed information in respect of the expenditure. As Justice Woods confirmed at the Federal Court of Appeal, the information must be provided by the taxpayer on the prescribed form. Relying on Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd v The Queen, 2016 FCA 301, Justice Miller held that the Minister is not required to look into another taxpayer’s file to ascertain the prescribed information needed to cure a deficient Form T661.

Moreover, from a technical SR&ED compliance perspective, intra-group collaboration between a management holding company and an operating subsidiary presents acute substantive risks even when narratives are filed. Westsource’s primary business was providing management services to its subsidiaries. Routine management services, corporate administration, financial oversight, and general executive direction do not qualify as SR&ED under subsection 248(1). For two collaborating related corporations to claim separate SR&ED expenditures on the same underlying project (without triggering intercompany contract exclusion rules or duplicate claims), each corporation’s Form T661 must specifically articulate the technological uncertainties addressed and the systematic investigation performed by or on behalf of that specific claimant during the taxation year. Relying passively on a subsidiary's narrative leaves the parent company unable to demonstrate how its own personnel directly performed experimental development or commensurate support work under paragraph (d) of the SR&ED definition in subsection 248(1).
Expiration of the Statutory Filing Window and Absence of Equitable Relief

The final failure was procedural timing: Westsource submitted its SR&ED claim via an amended return for the 2011 taxation year and failed to detect or cure the missing Schedule 60 narratives prior to the expiration of the twelve-month filing deadline under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m). Under the Canadian SR&ED regime, a taxpayer has twelve months past its T2 filing-due date (creating a total window of eighteen months from the end of the taxation year for a corporation) to submit a complete Form T661. While a taxpayer may amend or supplement a Form T661 freely within that eighteen-month window, the window closes with absolute finality on the statutory bar date.

When Westsource filed its amended return without completing Boxes 240, 242, and 244 for Project 1, and allowed the twelve-month deadline under subsection 37(11) to lapse, the deduction-denial rule then contained in subsection 37(11) (now housed in subsection 37(11.1)) and the deeming provision in subsection 37(12) were irreversibly triggered. Once triggered, the Project 1 expenditures (in respect of which a refundable ITC of $29,504 had been claimed) were statutorily barred from deduction under subsection 37(1) and excluded from the definition of "qualified expenditure" for ITC purposes under subsection 127(9). Before the Tax Court, Westsource argued that the Minister’s position was overly simplistic and frustrated Parliament’s intent in enacting the SR&ED program, and before the Federal Court of Appeal it suggested that the result was harsh in its particular circumstances, to which that Court responded that relief cannot be provided on the basis of fairness alone. However, the Tax Court of Canada is a statutory court governed by the Tax Court of Canada Act and the Income Tax Act; it is not a court of equity and possesses no inherent jurisdiction to waive mandatory statutory filing deadlines or grant relief on the basis of fairness alone.
Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and legal requirement examined in Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 9; aff'd 2018 FCA 57) against the taxpayer’s specific failure and the governing judicial standard of proof established by the courts.

headers: Judicial Standard of Proof & Legal Holding

cells: ITA Subsection 37(11) & Paragraph 127(9)(m): Mandatory filing of a prescribed form (Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31) containing prescribed information within 12 months of the taxpayer's T2 filing-due date.

Westsource filed an amended 2011 tax return claiming SR&ED expenditures and refundable ITCs for Project 1 (refundable ITC claimed: $29,504) and Project 2 (refundable ITC claimed: $26,894), but left Boxes 240, 242, and 244 of Schedule 60 (Part 2 of Form T661) completely blank for Project 1 prior to the 12-month statutory deadline.

Strict Statutory Compliance: Filing a Form T661 with financial figures alone does not satisfy subsection 37(11). Every project claimed must be accompanied by a completed Part 2 (Schedule 60) containing all required technical descriptions on or before the 12-month bar date.
ITA Subsection 248(1) & Subsection 244(16): Definition of "prescribed" in relation to forms and information to be given on a form as "authorized by the Minister".

Westsource argued that because no regulation in the Income Tax Regulations defined "prescribed information" for subsection 37(11), the phrase was ambiguous and did not encompass the narrative boxes on Form T661.

Ministerial Authorization Standard: Under subsection 248(1), "prescribed" regarding information to be given on a form means authorized by the Minister, not prescribed by Governor in Council regulation. Because Form T661 is authorized by the Minister and explicitly states that all requested fields are prescribed information, Boxes 240, 242, and 244 are statutorily prescribed.

ITA Subsection 248(1) (SR&ED Definition) & Form T661 Part 2 (Boxes 240, 242, 244 / Modern Lines 242, 244, 246): Prima facie demonstration of technological advancement, technological uncertainty, and systematic investigation.

Westsource failed to articulate on its own Form T661 what technological advancements were sought (Box 240), what technological obstacles existed (Box 242), and what systematic investigation was performed in 2011 (Box 244) for Project 1.

Substantive Core Standard: The Court held that Boxes 240, 242, and 244 go "to the heart of whether the claim made is SR&ED". Without these three narratives on the form, the Minister cannot determine from the filing whether the activity meets the substantive statutory definition in subsection 248(1).
Separate Corporate Personality & Intra-Group Collaborations (ITA Section 2 & Subsection 37(11)): Each corporate taxpayer must independently satisfy filing requirements on its own tax return.

Westsource argued that the missing narratives were unnecessary because it had collaborated on Project 1 with a related corporation, WestSource Solutions Inc., that the Minister could have found the missing information in the Form T661 filed on behalf of that corporation, and (before the Federal Court of Appeal) that the related corporation’s claims for the project had been accepted by the Minister.

Strict Taxpayer-Specific Filing: The Minister is not required to look into another taxpayer’s file to ascertain the claimant’s prescribed information (Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd v The Queen, 2016 FCA 301), and the Minister’s possession of relevant project information through a related corporation’s return does not relieve the claimant corporation of its statutory duty. The prescribed information must be provided by the taxpayer on its own prescribed form.

ITA Subsections 37(12) & 37(11.1): Deeming provision / statutory bar disallowing any deduction under subsection 37(1) where prescribed information is omitted, and interaction with equitable fairness arguments.

Westsource contended that the Minister’s position was overly simplistic and frustrated Parliament’s intent, that "prescribed information" should be interpreted liberally given the purpose of the SR&ED incentives, that budgetary material showed the filing requirement was simply meant to deny retroactive claims, and that the result was harsh in its particular circumstances.

Mandatory Disallowance & No Equitable Jurisdiction: Where statutory language is clear and unambiguous, a general statement of legislative intent in budget material cannot take precedence over the Act, and the Federal Court of Appeal found its interpretation consistent with the administrative policy statements to which it was referred. The deduction-denial rule (formerly in subsection 37(11), now subsection 37(11.1)) and the deeming rule in subsection 37(12) mandate total disallowance, subsection 220(2.2) removes the Minister’s authority to waive the requirement, and the Courts cannot grant relief on the basis of fairness alone.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the judicial principles of Westsource Group Holdings Inc. into actionable tax and technical risk management, the following two applied industry case studies examine realistic Canadian corporate taxpayers confronting the exact legal, structural, and procedural pitfalls identified by the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal. Each case study provides a rigorous, step-by-step remedial framework covering project governance, technical documentation, contractual architecture, and experimentation tracking.
Case Study 1: Multi-Entity Corporate Group & Intercompany Collaboration in Agricultural IoT Manufacturing
Scenario & Identified Westsource Pitfalls

PrairieAgri Holdings Inc. ("PrairieHoldings") is a privately held management and holding corporation headquartered in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, owning 100% of the voting shares of PrairieSeeding Technologies Ltd. ("PrairieTech"), an agricultural machinery and precision-sensor manufacturing corporation. Like the Appellant in Westsource, PrairieHoldings provides general management services to its subsidiary, PrairieTech; in addition, PrairieHoldings employs two senior mechanical engineers and a Chief Technology Officer (who is also a "specified employee" owning 15% of PrairieHoldings).

During its fiscal year ended December 31, 2025, PrairieHoldings and PrairieTech collaborated on "Project Precision-Depth," an experimental development initiative aimed at overcoming severe hydraulic pressure oscillations and acoustic sensor signal attenuation in high-speed pneumatic seed drills operating in frozen, high-clay soil conditions. PrairieHoldings incurred $145,000 in senior engineering wages and prototype Finite Element Analysis (FEA) software costs, while PrairieTech incurred $420,000 in shop-floor prototype fabrication, sensor assembly, and field-testing wages.

When preparing the 2025 T2 returns, the corporate group’s external accountant completed a full Part 2 (Schedule 60) technical narrative on PrairieTech’s Form T661 (Lines 242, 244, and 246). However, on PrairieHoldings’ Form T661, the accountant entered the $145,000 expenditure in Part 3 and Part 4 to claim the enhanced 35% refundable ITC, but left Part 2 (Lines 242, 244, and 246) blank—inserting only a single line in the project title field reading: "See Joint Project Precision-Depth filed under subsidiary PrairieSeeding Technologies Ltd. BN 123456789RC0001". Furthermore, the intercompany agreement between PrairieHoldings and PrairieTech simply describes PrairieHoldings’ activities as "executive management and technical oversight services" billed via a flat monthly management fee.

If filed in this state and allowed to pass the eighteen-month statutory bar date (June 30, 2027), PrairieHoldings’ $145,000 SR&ED claim will be summarily disallowed under subsections 37(11), 37(11.1), and 37(12) pursuant to the Westsource precedent. Even if spotted prior to the bar date, the ambiguous "management services" contract and undivided technical narrative expose both entities to disqualification regarding who actually performed the systematic investigation and whether intercompany payments constitute non-qualifying management fees or unallocated contract payments.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Project Governance & Multi-Entity SR&ED Tax Structuring

To eliminate the Westsource collaborative filing defect, PrairieHoldings and PrairieTech must establish formal intra-group SR&ED governance prior to fiscal year-end that deliberately selects between two legally compliant structural pathways under section 37 and section 127 of the Act. Under the first pathway—a consolidated claimant structure via an intercompany SR&ED subcontract—if the corporate group prefers to prepare and defend a primary claim in the operating subsidiary, PrairieTech can act as the primary SR&ED claimant and contract with PrairieHoldings to perform specific engineering and FEA simulation tasks on PrairieTech's behalf, as SR&ED directly undertaken on behalf of PrairieTech under paragraph 37(1)(a) of the Act. Because PrairieHoldings and PrairieTech do not deal at arm's length, paragraph (f) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) and subsections 127(13) to 127(17) of the Act govern the ITC calculation: the intercompany contract payment does not directly generate ITCs for the payer unless the two corporations execute and timely file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) to transfer PrairieHoldings' qualified expenditures to PrairieTech. Crucially, even when utilizing Form T1146, the non-arm's-length performer (PrairieHoldings) is still statutorily required to calculate its underlying qualified SR&ED expenditures on its own Form T661, necessitating complete prescribed information on both returns.

Under the second pathway—bifurcated collaborative co-claimants—where both PrairieHoldings and PrairieTech file independent SR&ED claims for their respective un-reimbursed expenditures ($145,000 and $420,000) without intercompany billing for the R&D work, corporate governance must treat each entity as a completely standalone statutory claimant. Under the strict Westsource rule, PrairieHoldings cannot incorporate PrairieTech’s Form T661 by reference. The corporate tax committee must institute a mandatory pre-filing compliance gate requiring every legal entity claiming $1.00 or more of SR&ED expenditures to generate a complete, self-contained Schedule 60 (Part 2 of Form T661) within its own T2 return.
Step 2: Technical Documentation & Form T661 Part 2 (Schedule 60) Narrative Architecture

Assuming PrairieHoldings proceeds as a collaborative co-claimant, it must populate every prescribed field in Part 2 of its own Form T661, specifically Lines 242, 244, and 246 (corresponding to Boxes 240, 242, and 244 in Westsource). While the overarching technological project is collaborative, PrairieHoldings’ Part 2 narrative must be customized to reflect the specific technological uncertainties, hypotheses, and systematic analysis conducted by PrairieHoldings’ own engineering staff, while explicitly contextualizing the collaboration with PrairieTech.

In completing Line 242 (Scientific or Technological Uncertainties, subject to the 350-word limit), PrairieHoldings must define the fundamental system-level uncertainty that could not be resolved through standard mechanical engineering or commercially available fluid-dynamics modeling. Specifically, the narrative must detail the inability of existing laminar-flow hydraulic equations and standard piezoelectric acoustic damping models to predict non-linear pressure spikes (hydraulic transients of up to 250 bar at 30–80 Hz) and ultrasonic backscatter interference when seeding coulters impact heterogeneous frozen clay-loam strata at ground speeds exceeding 12 km/h. Subsequently, in Line 244 (Work Performed in the Tax Year to Overcome Uncertainties, subject to the 700-word limit), PrairieHoldings must strictly segregate its own systematic investigation from PrairieTech’s shop-floor fabrication. The narrative must chronicle PrairieHoldings’ chronological hypotheses, multi-physics Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and FEA simulations, mathematical modeling of acoustic wave propagation through frozen soil matrices, and statistical regression analysis of telemetry data fed back from PrairieTech’s field test rigs. By documenting this analytical sequence, PrairieHoldings proves that its personnel performed direct experimental development and analysis under subsection 248(1), rather than non-eligible executive management.

In Line 246 (Scientific or Technological Advancements Achieved, subject to the 350-word limit), PrairieHoldings must articulate the new technological knowledge gained regarding coupled hydro-mechanical damping ratios and frequency-hopping acoustic signal filtering algorithms under sub-zero high-impact regimes. Finally, to satisfy the Westsource mandate that all fields on Form T661 constitute prescribed information, PrairieHoldings must complete all administrative and evidentiary checkboxes in Section A and Section C of Part 2, including project start and end dates (Lines 202 and 204), the field of science or technology code (Line 206), the indicator of whether the project was claimed in a previous year (Line 208), the indicator of joint or collaborative work confirming collaboration with PrairieTech (Line 218), and the contemporaneous evidence indicators in Lines 270 to 282.
Step 3: Contractual Terms & Intercompany Agreements

Because Westsource was a management holding company whose principal service was providing management services to its subsidiaries, any intercompany agreement between PrairieHoldings and PrairieTech must be surgically restructured to eliminate the characterization of PrairieHoldings’ engineers as performing routine management. First, the flat-fee Intercompany Management Services Agreement (covering accounting, human resources, legal, and general corporate governance) must be legally severed from a newly executed Intercompany Collaborative Research and Cost-Sharing Agreement. Second, the Collaborative Research Agreement must specify that PrairieHoldings bears its own financial risk for the $145,000 in computational modeling and algorithm design expenditures, without reimbursement or markup from PrairieTech (unless a formal Form T1146 transfer is elected), and that both corporations hold joint beneficial ownership rights to exploit the resulting intellectual property in Canada. Third, with respect to the CTO (a specified employee holding 15% of the shares of PrairieHoldings), employment contracts and payroll records must comply with the specified employee rules in subsections 37(9) to 37(9.5) of the Act, limiting his eligible SR&ED salary to the portion reasonably attributable to his direct SR&ED work and to the statutory cap of five times the Year’s Maximum Pensionable Earnings under subsection 37(9.1), excluding all bonuses or remuneration based on profits under subsection 37(9), and properly allocating the associated-corporation salary cap across both PrairieHoldings and PrairieTech through the agreement contemplated by subsections 37(9.2) to 37(9.4).
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking & Contemporaneous Evidence Protocols

To substantiate the prescribed information entered on Form T661 and satisfy Lines 270 to 282 of Part 2, PrairieHoldings must implement a bifurcated tracking and pre-filing verification protocol. PrairieHoldings’ engineers and CTO must log daily hours into an activity-based tracking ledger that explicitly separates non-eligible corporate management and commercial production support from eligible SR&ED mathematical modeling, hypothesis formulation, and test data analysis tied to specific experimental iterations in Line 244. Furthermore, in direct response to the procedural failure in Westsource, PrairieHoldings must implement an internal tax compliance control requiring that whenever an initial or amended T2 return includes Schedule T2SCH31, the tax software's electronic transmission file (.cor file) is audited by a senior tax advisor at least 60 days prior to the subsection 37(11) twelve-month deadline to verify that Schedule 60 (Part 2) contains populated text strings in Lines 242, 244, and 246 for every project listed in the expenditure schedule.
Case Study 2: High-Volume Multi-Project Software & FinTech Enterprise Filing an Amended Return Near the Statutory Bar Date
Scenario & Identified Westsource Pitfalls

QuantEdge FinTech Corp. ("QuantEdge") is a Toronto-based financial technology corporation developing high-frequency algorithmic liquidity routing engines and post-quantum cryptographic settlement protocols. For its taxation year ended June 30, 2025, QuantEdge initially filed its T2 return on time on December 31, 2025, without claiming SR&ED, as its engineering leadership was preoccupied with a Series B financing round.

In November 2026—just weeks before its absolute twelve-month SR&ED filing deadline of December 31, 2026 under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m)—QuantEdge engaged an external contingency-fee claim preparer to file an amended 2025 T2 return claiming $1,850,000 in SR&ED proxy-method expenditures across 24 distinct software development micro-projects. Under severe time pressure, the claim preparer drafted complete Part 2 narratives (Lines 242, 244, and 246) for the 4 largest projects (representing $750,000 of expenditures). However, for the remaining 20 smaller projects (representing $1,100,000 of expenditures), the preparer misunderstood the CRA’s T661 Top 20 Projects administrative software limitation and also assumed that because 12 of those projects were continuations of projects reviewed and approved by the CRA in the 2024 taxation year, the CRA already possessed the relevant technical background. Consequently, the preparer submitted the amended 2025 T661 with the full $1,850,000 expenditure total in Part 3, but included Part 2 schedules for only the top 4 projects—leaving out Part 2 schedules or leaving Lines 242, 244, and 246 blank for the other 20 projects—and also omitted part of the mandatory claim preparer billing arrangement details in Part 9.

Under the strict legal holding in Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. The Queen, this filing is catastrophic. First, the CRA’s SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy requires every claimant to complete and keep a Part 2 (Schedule 60) for each project claimed; a claimant may submit Part 2 for only its 20 largest projects by dollar value, but Part 2 must be filed by the reporting deadline for each of those 20 projects, and the CRA may request Part 2 for any remaining project, with the expenditures claimed for that project disallowed if it is not provided. Second, Westsource establishes that the Minister’s possession of relevant project information—there, through a related corporation’s accepted claim for the same project and the taxpayer’s own indication on its form that the project was a continuation from a prior year—does not relieve the taxpayer of its obligation under subsection 37(11) to provide the prescribed information on its own prescribed form for the current taxation year; this is particularly true because Box 244 (modern Line 244) specifically requires a description of the systematic investigation performed in the current taxation year. Once December 31, 2026 passes, the expenditures for the 16 undescribed projects that rank among QuantEdge’s 20 largest will be permanently disallowed under subsections 37(11.1) and 37(12), with zero recourse to the Tax Court of Canada, and the expenditures for the 4 smallest projects will be disallowed if the CRA requests their Part 2 and QuantEdge cannot provide it.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Project Governance & Technical Project Aggregation Strategy

The root operational flaw in QuantEdge’s claim preparation is defining every granular Agile software epic or sprint as a standalone SR&ED "project," resulting in 24 fragmented claims that cannot be properly documented before the statutory deadline. Under the CRA’s SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy and the Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, an SR&ED project is defined at the level of a cohesive scientific or technological advancement aimed at resolving a core set of interrelated technological uncertainties, rather than at the level of commercial product features or individual software sprints.

Before filing the amended 2025 return on or before December 31, 2026, QuantEdge must restructure its project governance by aggregating the 24 fragmented software micro-projects into three overarching, technologically cohesive SR&ED projects based on the underlying computer science domains. The first consolidated project—Ultra-Low-Latency Kernel-Bypass Routing Architecture—combines nine micro-projects addressing non-deterministic memory contention and lock-free ring-buffer thread synchronization in multi-core NUMA architectures under extreme packet bursts. The second consolidated project—Lattice-Based Post-Quantum Cryptographic Handshake Optimization—aggregates eight micro-projects addressing computational overhead and state-synchronization failures when embedding CRYSTALS-Kyber key encapsulation mechanisms into sub-millisecond FIX financial messaging protocols. The third consolidated project—Stochastic Order-Book Liquidity Prediction Engine—combines seven micro-projects addressing numerical instability and vanishing gradients in real-time non-stationary spatiotemporal graph neural networks. By consolidating 24 feature-level fragments into three legitimate technological projects, QuantEdge eliminates the administrative burden of preparing 24 separate Part 2 schedules while aligning its claim structure directly with the statutory criteria of subsection 248(1).
Step 2: Technical Documentation & Form T661 Compliance Controls

For each of the three consolidated projects—including those continuing from the 2024 taxation year—QuantEdge must draft and embed complete prescribed information in Part 2 (Schedule 60) of its 2025 Form T661 prior to the December 31, 2026 bar date. In strict adherence to Westsource, QuantEdge must prohibit any narrative shortcuts that refer the CRA to its 2024 Form T661 filing or 2024 audit binder. Even for multi-year continuation projects where Line 208 is checked "Yes," the 2025 Form T661 must independently contain the full prescribed text in Lines 242, 244, and 246. For continuing projects, the narrative in Line 244 (historical Box 244) must specifically isolate the technological obstacles that remained unresolved as of July 1, 2024, and detail the exact hypotheses formulated, algorithmic architectures coded, load-test benchmarks executed, and failure analyses conducted between July 1, 2024 and June 30, 2025. Furthermore, every dollar of the $1,850,000 claimed in Part 3 must be explicitly mapped to Project 1, Project 2, or Project 3 on Schedule 60, ensuring that no "orphan" expenditures exist on the return without an accompanying completed Part 2 narrative.
Step 3: Contractual Terms & Claim Preparer Statutory Governance

Because QuantEdge engaged an external contingency-fee consultant and utilized third-party software contractors during 2025, its contractual and statutory governance must address two critical provisions of section 37. First, as reflected in the modern statutory structure of subsection 37(11), a compliant filing requires both "(a) prescribed information in respect of the expenditure" and "(b) claim preparer information, as defined in subsection 162(5.3)". QuantEdge’s engagement agreement with its SR&ED consultant must contractually obligate the preparer to provide its CRA Business Number, billing arrangement code, contingency fee percentage, and total fee structure for complete disclosure in Part 9 of Form T661, alongside executing a joint accuracy certification prior to filing. Second, to ensure that payments to third-party Canadian software developers qualify as SR&ED directly undertaken on QuantEdge's behalf under paragraph 37(1)(a) (eligible at 80% for ITC purposes), all Statements of Work (SOWs) must explicitly stipulate that the contractor is performing experimental development under QuantEdge’s technical direction, that all intellectual property vests exclusively in QuantEdge upon creation, and that QuantEdge retains the sole contractual right to claim SR&ED tax incentives in respect of the contracted work.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking & Statutory Deadline Risk Management

To prevent late-stage amended return crises like that in Westsource, QuantEdge must institutionalize an automated experimentation tracking and statutory calendar protocol. On the technical side, QuantEdge must configure its Jira issue-tracking and Git version-control repositories with dedicated SR&ED taxonomy tags mapping directly to Lines 270 to 282 of Form T661, so that at the end of each quarterly engineering cycle, automated scripts extract failed commit logs, latency profiling benchmarks, and architectural post-mortems into a contemporaneous evidence dossier that directly populates draft narratives for Lines 242, 244, and 246. On the tax governance side, corporate policy must prohibit holding SR&ED claims for post-filing T2 amendments. All SR&ED schedules (Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31) must be prepared concurrently with the original T2 return due six months after fiscal year-end. In any exceptional circumstance where an amended return is required, a mandatory legal and technical pre-filing audit must be completed no later than 15 months after fiscal year-end (90 days prior to the absolute 18-month statutory bar date under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m)), verifying line-by-line that every field on Form T661 contains complete, self-contained prescribed information.
Summary of Practice Directives for Canadian Tax Advisors

The rulings of the Tax Court of Canada (2017 TCC 9) and the Federal Court of Appeal (2018 FCA 57) in Westsource Group Holdings Inc. serve as an uncompromising warning to Canadian corporate taxpayers, Chief Financial Officers, and SR&ED claim preparers. Under the Canadian Income Tax Act, the filing of Form T661 is not a flexible administrative formality; it is a strict statutory condition precedent to the deductibility of expenditures under subsection 37(1) and the generation of Investment Tax Credits under subsection 127(9).

Every field on Form T661—most notably the technical project narratives in Part 2 (Lines 242, 244, and 246, formerly Boxes 240, 242, and 244)—constitutes "prescribed information" authorized by the Minister pursuant to the definition of "prescribed" in subsection 248(1), as confirmed by the instructions on Form T661 itself. Canadian practitioners must operate under the absolute rule that each corporate entity within a corporate group is evaluated in strict legal isolation, that the CRA’s prior or collateral knowledge of a project will never cure an incomplete Form T661, and that once the twelve-month post-filing-due-date window under subsection 37(11) closes, neither the Minister nor the Tax Court of Canada can rescue an incomplete claim on equitable grounds.

outcome: Appeal dismissed; TCC held prescribed project information on Form T661 must be filed within 12 months of the filing-due date.
